source: CARE Cambodia (Pailin), "TIP Training on Maize Production" / បទដ្ឋានអនុវត្ដបច្ចេកវិទ្យា ផលិតកម្មដំណំពូតក្របម, 2009. Funded by AusAID (ACIMA project), the European Union (Pailin Food Security Program), and ACIAR (CCPMP project).
text:
Glyphosate is one of the two most commonly used weed-killer types for corn production in Cambodia (locally referred to in the Pailin area as "ទឹកខ្មៅ", Teuk Khmao). It is a non-selective, systemic herbicide that kills nearly all plant types it contacts, including grasses, corn, beans, potato, and other crops — it does not distinguish between weed species, so it must not be allowed to contact any desired crop.

Timing and method: it should be sprayed onto weeds/vegetation before final ploughing or before planting the crop.

Mode of action: it works systemically by translocation — once any part of a weed absorbs the chemical, it moves down through the plant to the root system, killing the weed at the root within about 5-10 days after application. Weeds should not be cut/mowed before spraying, because the product must be absorbed through the leaves and stems to translocate effectively.

Toxicity: it has low toxicity to humans, and it becomes inactive once it contacts soil. Clean water must be used to mix the herbicide (not dirty/muddy water), since dirty water reduces the product's effectiveness.

Rainfastness: after spraying, the product needs about 4-6 hours of dry weather to be absorbed into the weed. If rain falls less than 4 hours after spraying, it will wash off the chemical and reduce its effectiveness.
